title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation: likelihood, score and properties
breadcrumb: Statistical Inference → Point Estimation → Maximum likelihood
engineName: Estimation and inference — let the observed data tell us which parameter value fits best
provenance: New lesson prepared to close the missing inference-t4 learning coverage identified during the supplementary question-bank audit (November 2026). Scope follows Unit IV of the supplied UGC NET Statistics syllabus: maximum likelihood estimators and their relationship to point-estimation properties. Examples are original instructional examples, not represented as official PYQs. The linked supplementary pool is separately labelled practice material.
objectives: Build a likelihood from a sample and distinguish a likelihood function from a probability distribution.
Find an MLE by taking logarithms, differentiating the log-likelihood and checking that the candidate is a maximum.
Handle common models: Bernoulli, Poisson, exponential, normal and uniform distributions.
Use the invariance property to estimate a function of a parameter.
Recognise boundary, constrained and non-unique MLEs, and cases where an MLE does not exist in the stated parameter space.
Distinguish bias, consistency, efficiency and asymptotic properties; avoid claiming that every MLE is unbiased or best in finite samples.

prereq.name: Probability mass and density functions
prereq.why: The likelihood is built from the sample's joint probability mass or density. Be comfortable multiplying independent probabilities or densities.

prereq.name: Logarithms, differentiation and maxima
prereq.why: The main computational method is to maximise the log-likelihood. Logarithms simplify products, while derivatives locate interior candidates.

prereq.name: Random samples, expectation and variance
prereq.why: Bias and consistency are properties of the estimator across repeated samples, not properties of one observed numerical answer.

sheet: Likelihood: L(θ;x) = f(x₁,…,xₙ;θ). For an iid sample, L(θ;x) = ∏ᵢ f(xᵢ;θ).
An MLE maximises L(θ;x) over the allowed parameter space Θ. The observed data are fixed; θ is the variable being maximised.
Log-likelihood: ℓ(θ) = log L(θ). Since log is increasing, maximising ℓ and L gives the same maximiser.
Interior score equation: U(θ) = dℓ(θ)/dθ = 0. Check the second derivative or compare likelihood values and boundary points.
Bernoulli(p): p̂ = X̄. Poisson(λ): λ̂ = X̄.
Exponential(rate λ): λ̂ = 1/X̄ = n/ΣXᵢ. Do not confuse rate and scale.
Normal(μ,σ²), both unknown: μ̂ = X̄ and σ̂² = (1/n)Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². The MLE variance uses n, not n−1.
Uniform(0,θ): θ̂ = X₍ₙ₎, the sample maximum. Support restrictions matter.
Invariance: if θ̂ is an MLE, then g(θ̂) is an MLE of g(θ), under the induced-likelihood convention.
MLE need not be unbiased, unique, or attained inside an open parameter space.
Constrained MLE: maximise over the allowed parameter set; an unconstrained estimate outside the set is not permitted.
Large-sample theory often gives consistency and asymptotic normality under regularity conditions; these are not automatic in every model.
cards: What is the likelihood?
The joint probability or density of the observed sample, viewed as a function of the unknown parameter.
Why use the log-likelihood?
It turns products into sums and has the same maximiser because logarithm is strictly increasing.
What is the score?
The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter.
MLE of Bernoulli p?
The sample proportion of successes, X̄.
MLE of Poisson λ?
The sample mean, X̄.
MLE of exponential rate λ?
1/X̄. If the parameter is scale β instead, the MLE is X̄.
Why does normal MLE variance use n?
It maximises the likelihood. Dividing by n−1 is a bias correction for an unbiased estimator, not the MLE.
MLE for Uniform(0,θ)?
The sample maximum X₍ₙ₎, because θ must be at least as large as every observation and the likelihood decreases as θ grows.
Does an MLE always exist?
No. A likelihood may have only a supremum at an excluded boundary, or may fail to attain its maximum.
Does MLE invariance mean all estimators are invariant?
No. The invariance property applies to maximum likelihood estimation, not generally to unbiased or UMVU estimators.

tricks.why: The parameter space tells you whether the candidate is allowed and whether a boundary must be checked.
Take logarithms before differentiating; this reduces algebra and avoids repeated product rules.
For an exponential distribution the rate MLE is 1/X̄, while the scale MLE is X̄.
The likelihood maximiser for a normal variance uses divisor n. The familiar n−1 belongs to the unbiased sample variance.

tricks.hook: Score zero is only a candidate
tricks.why: A stationary point can be a minimum or saddle point; check curvature and boundaries.

shortcuts: Bernoulli and Poisson: the MLE is the sample mean.
Normal with both parameters unknown: μ̂ = X̄ and σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n.
To estimate g(θ), apply g to the MLE when the usual invariance conditions apply.
remember: An MLE is a parameter value that makes the observed sample most likely under the model; it is not the probability that the parameter is true.
Always check the parameter space, support and boundary after solving the score equation.
Unbiasedness and maximum likelihood are different ideas. An MLE can be biased and still be consistent.

traps: Treating L(θ;x) as a probability distribution over θ. It is a function of θ for fixed observed data.
Maximising the likelihood with respect to the observations instead of the unknown parameter.
Using a score equation without checking whether the solution is inside the parameter space.
Using n−1 for the normal maximum-likelihood variance estimator.
Assuming a supremum at an excluded boundary is an attained MLE.
Applying invariance to UMVUEs or arbitrary estimators.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — the probability facts we need
scenes.objective: Recall how a random sample produces a joint probability or density.
body: Maximum likelihood starts with a simple question: for the data we actually observed, which parameter value makes those data most plausible under the model? Before answering it, we need the joint distribution of a sample.

items.ask: If X₁,…,Xₙ are independent, how do we write their joint density?
refresh: Independence lets us multiply probabilities or densities. This product, with the observed x-values inserted, becomes the likelihood function.

items.ask: What is the difference between a parameter and an observation?
items.recall: The observations are the realised data. The parameter θ is an unknown fixed quantity in the model that we want to estimate.
refresh: In likelihood calculations, the observations are held fixed and we vary θ. This is the key change in viewpoint.

items.ask: What does a derivative equal to zero tell us?
items.recall: It identifies an interior stationary point, which still needs to be checked as a maximum.
refresh: A zero derivative alone does not prove a maximum. We also check the second derivative or compare the likelihood at possible boundaries.

scenes.title: The central idea — which parameter best explains the data?
scenes.objective: Interpret likelihood as a score for parameter values given fixed observations.
body: Imagine a coin has an unknown probability p of landing heads. You toss it 10 times and observe 7 heads. If p=0.7, this result is quite plausible. If p=0.1, seven heads would be much less plausible. Maximum likelihood chooses the p that gives the largest probability to the observed data.
The likelihood is not the probability that p is true. It is the probability of the observed data, calculated under each proposed p. We compare those values and choose the largest.

scenario.teaser: A coin is tossed ten times and seven heads appear.
scenario.title: Why the sample proportion is the most plausible value
body: A student is trying to estimate the chance that a particular coin lands heads. She does not know whether the coin is fair, so she tosses it ten times and records seven heads and three tails. Several possible values of p can be considered. If p is very close to zero, observing seven heads would be surprising. If p is very close to one, observing three tails would be surprising. A value around 0.7 makes the observed balance of heads and tails most plausible.

The likelihood function puts a numerical score on each proposed value of p. It is not a statement that p itself has a probability. We hold the ten observations fixed and compare the probability of getting this exact pattern under different values of p. The maximum-likelihood estimate is the value that gives the largest score.
scenario.q: What value of p makes the observed 7 heads in 10 tosses most likely?

scenes.title: A likelihood you can calculate by hand
scenes.objective: See why the sample proportion maximises the Bernoulli likelihood.

viz.caption: Likelihood shape for a binomial sample: the maximum occurs at the observed proportion.

body: For 7 heads and 3 tails, the likelihood is proportional to p⁷(1−p)³. The constant combination count does not depend on p, so it cannot change the maximiser.
The likelihood is small near p=0 because heads were observed, and small near p=1 because tails were also observed. It peaks at p=0.7.

scenes.title: Construct the likelihood and use the log
scenes.objective: Write the likelihood for an iid sample and obtain the score equation.

blocks.body: For observed data x₁,…,xₙ from a model with parameter θ, define L(θ;x)=f(x₁,…,xₙ;θ). For independent observations this is the product of the individual densities or mass functions.
ℓ(θ)=log L(θ;x)=Σᵢ log f(xᵢ;θ). The logarithm is strictly increasing, so L and ℓ have the same maximiser.
For a differentiable one-parameter model, calculate U(θ)=dℓ(θ)/dθ and solve U(θ)=0 for interior candidates.

blocks.h: A candidate is not yet an answer
blocks.body: Check the second derivative, compare possible endpoints and verify that the candidate belongs to the parameter space Θ.

Differentiability, interchange of differentiation and integration, and parameter-independent support are common regularity conditions in standard large-sample theory. They do not hold in every model, especially some uniform-support models.

flow.title: The maximum-likelihood workflow
flow.alt: Start with the model and observed sample, construct the joint likelihood, take its logarithm, solve the score equation, check curvature and boundaries, then report the allowed maximiser.
flow.note: If the candidate is outside the parameter space or the likelihood has a boundary maximum, do not stop at the score equation.

scenes.title: Worked example 1 — Bernoulli probability
scenes.objective: Derive the MLE of a success probability from the likelihood.
scenes.problem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ comes from Bernoulli(p). Find the MLE of p.

steps.say: For one observation, P(Xᵢ=xᵢ)=pˣⁱ(1−p)^(1−xᵢ), where xᵢ is either 0 or 1.
Differentiate and set the score equal to zero.
Multiply by p(1−p) and solve: Σxᵢ(1−p)=p(n−Σxᵢ), so Σxᵢ=np.

The second derivative is negative for 0<p<1, so this interior stationary point is a maximum when 0<Σxᵢ<n. If all observations are 0 or all are 1, the maximum is at the corresponding boundary if that boundary is included.

scenes.after: The MLE is the observed proportion of successes. This result is also the intuitive answer from the coin example.

scenes.title: Three standard models — remember the likelihood pattern
scenes.objective: Recognise the Poisson and exponential likelihoods quickly.
scenes.intro: For each model, write the log-likelihood first. Notice how the sufficient sample summary appears naturally.

items.q: For iid Poisson(λ), what is the log-likelihood up to terms not involving λ?
items.a: ℓ(λ)=−nλ+(Σxᵢ)log λ + constant. The score gives λ̂=X̄.

items.q: For iid exponential observations with rate λ, what is the MLE?
items.a: The likelihood is λⁿexp(−λΣxᵢ), so λ̂=n/Σxᵢ=1/X̄.

items.q: If the exponential is parameterised by scale β with density β⁻¹exp(−x/β), what is the MLE?
items.a: β̂=X̄. The rate and scale are reciprocals, so do not carry the rate formula over unchanged.

scenes.title: Normal distribution — why the divisor is n
scenes.objective: Derive the normal MLEs and distinguish the variance MLE from the unbiased estimator.

blocks.body: For fixed σ², maximising the likelihood is equivalent to minimising Σ(xᵢ−μ)². Differentiating gives μ̂=X̄.
Substitute μ̂=X̄ into the likelihood and differentiate with respect to σ². The result is σ̂²=Σ(xᵢ−X̄)²/n.
The unbiased sample variance divides by n−1. The maximum-likelihood estimator divides by n and is biased downward for finite n.
If μ is known, the MLE becomes σ̂²=Σ(xᵢ−μ)²/n. Use the known mean, not the sample mean.

scenes.title: Worked example 2 — normal variance
scenes.objective: Calculate the normal MLE variance from a small sample.
scenes.problem: Suppose the observations are 1, 2 and 3 from a normal population with unknown mean and variance. Find the MLEs.

steps.say: The sample mean is (1+2+3)/3=2, so μ̂=2.
Calculate the squared deviations from 2: (1−2)²=1, (2−2)²=0 and (3−2)²=1.
Add them: the sum of squared deviations is 2.
Divide by n=3 for the MLE variance.
The unbiased sample variance would be 2/(3−1)=1. These are different estimators because they answer different optimisation and bias questions.

scenes.after: Always identify whether the question asks for the MLE or the unbiased estimator.

scenes.title: Support, boundaries and constrained MLEs
scenes.objective: Handle uniform models and understand why the support can determine the MLE.

blocks.body: The parameter space Θ lists allowed parameter values. The support tells us which observations are possible for each parameter. A likelihood is zero whenever the observed sample is impossible under that parameter.
For iid observations from Uniform(0,θ), L(θ)=θ^(−n) when θ≥X₍ₙ₎ and zero otherwise. On the allowed region θ^(−n) decreases as θ increases, so θ̂=X₍ₙ₎.

If the likelihood increases towards a boundary that is excluded from Θ, it may have a supremum but no attained maximum. In that case an MLE does not exist in the stated parameter space. If Θ=(0,1) and every Bernoulli observation is a success, the likelihood pⁿ increases towards 1 but 1 is excluded. Its supremum is approached but not attained, so no MLE exists in that open parameter space.
First find the unconstrained candidate. Then restrict attention to Θ: if the candidate is outside, compare the allowed boundary or nearest feasible maximiser. Do not report a forbidden value.

scenes.title: Worked example 3 — a constrained Bernoulli model
scenes.objective: Project an unconstrained MLE onto a restricted parameter interval.
scenes.problem: Two Bernoulli observations are 0 and 1. The parameter is restricted to 1/3≤p≤2/3. Find the MLE.

steps.say: Without the restriction, the Bernoulli MLE is the sample proportion X̄=(0+1)/2=1/2.
Check the parameter space: 1/2 lies between 1/3 and 2/3.
Therefore the restriction does not change the maximiser.
If both observations were 0, the unconstrained maximiser would be 0, outside the interval. The constrained maximum would then occur at p=1/3.

scenes.title: Functions of parameters and invariance
scenes.objective: Apply the MLE invariance property correctly.

blocks.body: If θ̂ maximises the likelihood for θ, then g(θ̂) maximises the induced likelihood for g(θ), under the usual definition of the induced parameter likelihood.
If X₁,…,Xₙ are exponential with rate λ, λ̂=1/X̄. The MLE of the mean 1/λ is 1/λ̂=X̄.
The invariance property is a property of maximum likelihood estimators. It does not say that a transformation of an unbiased estimator remains unbiased or UMVU.

scenes.title: Guided practice — Poisson likelihood
scenes.objective: Derive a Poisson MLE without skipping algebra.
scenes.problem: For an iid sample from Poisson(λ), show that the MLE is X̄.
hints: Write the pmf for one observation: e^(−λ)λˣ/x!.
Multiply over i and take logarithms.
Differentiate with respect to λ and set the score to zero.
scenes.check: The score is −n + (Σxᵢ)/λ. For the sample mean 2, the MLE is λ̂=2, not n/λ.

solution.say: The likelihood is the product of the Poisson pmfs.
Differentiate and set equal to zero.

The second derivative is −Σxᵢ/λ², which is negative when the sample total is positive. If the total is zero, the likelihood is maximised at the boundary λ=0 if zero is included in the parameter space.

scenario.teaser: A quality-control team estimates the failure rate of a component.
scenario.title: Choosing a rate model for component lifetimes
body: A factory tests a batch of electronic components and records the time each component operates before failure. The engineering team assumes, as a first model, that lifetimes are independent and exponentially distributed with an unknown failure rate λ. The observed operating times are treated as fixed data while the team compares possible values of λ. A larger λ means failures tend to happen sooner; a smaller λ means longer operating times are more plausible.

The likelihood combines the exponential density for every observed lifetime. The log-likelihood turns the product into a sum, and differentiating gives an estimate based on the total operating time. This example also illustrates why parameterisation matters: the MLE of the failure rate is the reciprocal of the sample mean, whereas the MLE of the mean lifetime (the scale) is the sample mean itself.
scenario.q: If the sample mean lifetime is 12 hours, what is the MLE of the failure rate λ?

scenes.title: Complete the reasoning — exponential rate
scenes.objective: Practise the score equation for the exponential rate parameter.
scenes.problem: For iid exponential observations with rate λ, complete the likelihood calculation.

blank.prompt: Differentiate ℓ(λ) and set it to zero.
blank.hint: The derivative of n log λ is n/λ.

scenes.title: Trap check — five statements to judge
scenes.objective: Catch common mistakes about likelihood and MLE properties.
scenes.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false, then read the explanation.

items.claim: The likelihood is a probability distribution over the unknown parameter.
items.why: The likelihood is a function of the parameter for fixed observed data. It is not automatically a probability distribution over parameter values.

items.claim: Taking logarithms changes the maximum-likelihood estimate.
items.why: The logarithm is strictly increasing, so it preserves the location of the maximum.

items.claim: The normal MLE of variance uses divisor n.
items.why: The likelihood maximiser uses n. The n−1 divisor gives the unbiased sample variance.
For example, the normal MLE variance is biased downward for finite n.

items.claim: A zero score always proves that we have found an MLE.
items.why: It only gives an interior stationary candidate. Check curvature, boundaries and the parameter space.

scenes.title: The complete MLE checklist
scenes.objective: Consolidate the procedure and the standard results.
body: 1. Write the parameter space Θ and the model pmf/pdf.
2. Construct the joint likelihood, using independence when available.
3. Take logarithms to simplify the product.
4. Differentiate and solve the score equation for interior candidates.
5. Check the second derivative and every relevant boundary or support restriction.
6. State the estimator and its parameterisation clearly.
7. If asked about bias, consistency or efficiency, analyse those properties separately; they do not follow merely from maximising likelihood.
Core results: Bernoulli p̂=X̄; Poisson λ̂=X̄; exponential rate λ̂=1/X̄; normal μ̂=X̄ and σ̂²=Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)²/n; Uniform(0,θ) θ̂=X₍ₙ₎.

howto: Work through the scenes in order if likelihood is new to you. The foundation and intuition scenes rebuild the probability viewpoint; the worked scenes show the algebra line by line; the support and constraint scenes cover the cases where the score equation alone is not enough. If revising, use the revision sheet first, then attempt the guided scenes without hints. This lesson covers maximum likelihood estimation; sufficiency, completeness, Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé belong to the neighbouring inference topics.
